Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Central African Republic rely entirely on paper-based registers and forms for patient data recording at the point of care. The HMIS roadmap (2019) revised paper tools rolled out to 12 districts, with DHIS2 piloted only in Bangui (urban capital); no routine use in rural health centers (387 centers, 434 posts serving rural areas). World Bank SENI-PLUS (2022) notes plans for DHIS2 rollout but persistent barriers: poor internet connectivity, low staff capacity for data collection, weak data quality culture, insecurity from ongoing conflict.World Bank SENI-PLUS No national eHealth strategy exists (2023).Mayo Clinic Proceedings Recent donor-driven pilots like DHIS2-based immunization micro-planning exist but are isolated, not for patient records at POC.HISP Rwanda Key barriers: conflict (70% countryside outside govt control), infrastructure deficits, low capacity. National ambition for DHIS2 contrasts sharply with rural paper reality; data transcribed upward from paper, not captured digitally at facilities. No evidence majority rural clinics use digital systems routinely.

revision_notes: Original cited World Bank SENI-PLUS PAD (2022) was fetched and confirms DHIS2/HMIS rollout plans and persistent barriers (connectivity, capacity, insecurity). Fresh searches found a HISP WCA account (Aug 2024) of DHIS2 revitalisation showing the platform is used at district data-office level for Monthly Activity Report (RMA) data, not at facility level, with unstable internet and frequent power cuts still cited as obstacles. A 2025 IMPULSE multi-country study assessed DHIS2 functionality across 53 'data offices' at central and subnational level in CAR (fieldwork Nov 2022-Jul 2024), again confirming digitisation occurs upstream of the facility rather than at the point of care. No evidence of routine digital data capture in rural clinics themselves was found, so the score of 1 (Entirely paper) is confirmed.
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in the Central African Republic record patient data on paper at the point of care. The national DHIS2 rollout, begun in 2019 and expanded to pilot districts from 2022, digitises Monthly Activity Report (RMA) data at district data offices rather than at the clinic itself; clinics complete paper RMA forms which are later entered into DHIS2 upstream. Persistent barriers include unreliable internet connectivity, intermittent electricity, limited data-handling capacity and continuing insecurity across much of the countryside. A 2025 multi-country study of DHIS2 functionality found the system operating at 53 central and subnational data offices rather than at facility level. No routine digital data capture at the point of care has been identified in rural clinics.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: No evidence found of digital case management or record-keeping systems in rural Central African Republic (CAR) police stations or gendarmerie brigades. US State Department 2022 Human Rights Report notes poor recordkeeping of arrests/detentions, slow case processing due to understaffed/undertrained judicial police, and destruction of records in 2013 conflict, with rural stations (e.g., Bossembele, Boda) holding detainees in basic conditions. Complainants reportedly pay fees to file complaints. Recent UN MINUSCA donations (2025) of computers/printers/solar to rural Baoro station aim to facilitate drafting procès-verbaux/investigation reports, implying prior manual processes and suggesting transition from paper but not yet implemented widely. UK FCDO arrest pack and UNODC reports silent on digital tools; searches yielded no national police IT system for rural use. Ongoing conflict, infrastructure deficits, and aid focus on basics indicate entirely paper-based (or inadequate) systems in rural facilities.

revision_notes: The cited US State Department 2022 report URL now returns a technical/forbidden error and could not be re-verified directly; its substance is corroborated by other MINUSCA field reporting, so this does not change the assessment. Confirmed score of 1 (Entirely paper). MINUSCA field reports show that as recently as 2018 the mission was still distributing basic paper office registers ('registres de bureau') to police and gendarmerie units, and that as of June 2025 it delivered computers, printers and solar power to the rural Baoro police station and gendarmerie brigade specifically to help staff draft procès-verbaux and investigation reports that were previously handwritten - indicating this is the earliest stage of computerisation (equipment provision) rather than an operating digital case-management system. A similar 2024 donation to the Kaga-Bandoro gendarmerie paired computers with basic infrastructure (borehole, solar power). No evidence of an operating digital case-management or record-keeping system in rural stations was found.
revised_comments: Rural police stations and gendarmerie brigades in the Central African Republic continue to rely on paper-based registers and handwritten reports for case and detention records. MINUSCA has continued to supply basic paper registers to police and gendarmerie units and, as of mid-2025, has begun providing computers, printers and solar power to a small number of rural posts (including Baoro and Kaga-Bandoro) explicitly to help staff draft procès-verbaux and investigation reports that were previously handwritten. This reflects the earliest stage of computerisation - equipment provision rather than an operating digital case-management system - and rural stations remain entirely paper-based in practice, compounded by conflict-related insecurity and weak infrastructure across much of the country.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices in Central African Republic (secondary centres in villages) record births using paper forms and ledgers, with paper copies transferred throughout the system to central storage, per 2023 UNECA assessment of 43 African countries. No electronic CRVS database exists (one of 7 countries). FamilySearch confirms secondary centres in villages handle births, with no digital mention. World Bank ID4D (2017) details paper-based processes (loose-leaf/ledgers), no ICT (score 1/4); post-2013 crisis destroyed most rural offices, but surviving processes remain manual. Rural birth registration rates low (e.g., 36-63% 2000-2010). No evidence of digital rollout in recent (2020-2026) reports; one digital ministry (economy, 2026) unrelated. CDC older report notes subnational centres d'état civil, low completeness. Entirely paper-based in rural facilities.

revision_notes: Confirmed score of 1 (Entirely paper). The cited AfDB/COMESA digitalisation assessment (fetched, dated April 2023) was verified and lists the Central African Republic among African countries with no electronic CRVS database. FamilySearch's civil registration guide (last updated 2025) confirms secondary registration centres in villages and health facilities handle births/deaths with no digital system described. A 2024 UNICEF account of birth registration support in rural Lim-Pende prefecture describes a manual administrative process (paper certificates, supplementary judgements for late registration) with no digital capture at the registration point, corroborating continued reliance on paper at rural registry offices.
revised_comments: Rural civil registry offices in the Central African Republic - secondary registration centres located in villages and at health facilities - record births, deaths and marriages using paper forms and ledgers, with no electronic CRVS database in place. A 2023 continent-wide digitalisation assessment lists the country among those without an electronic civil registration database. UNICEF-supported birth registration activity in rural prefectures continues to rely on paper certificates and manual administrative procedures, such as supplementary judgements for late registrations, reflecting continued reliance on paper records at the point of registration. This is compounded by damage to registry infrastructure since the 2013 crisis and persistently low rural registration rates.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: No direct evidence on rural primary school data recording methods found despite extensive searches on EMIS, school data collection, UNESCO/World Bank/GPE documents. CAR participates in regional EMIS efforts and has a national system, but given ongoing conflict, low ICT infrastructure, and plans to strengthen data systems (PSE 2020-2029), rural facilities predominantly or entirely use paper registers for attendance, enrollment, grades, and admin data. 2007 World Bank survey highlights ICT challenges in education; recent reports note limited learning data availability.
redteam_note: No data year recorded - must be populated during verification.
revision_notes: Revised from 1 (Entirely paper) to 2 (Mostly paper - some digital). A Global Partnership for Education Independent Technical Appraisal Panel report (2023) confirms an Education Management Information System (EMIS) supported by EduTrac, introduced in 2019, under which school principals - not only in Bangui - transmit enrolment/attendance-type data in real time to a central web-based platform by SMS message. This constitutes digital data capture occurring at the school itself, even though detailed pupil records (attendance registers, grade books) remain paper-based day to day. This is a moderate, evidence-based one-step upgrade, not a promotion to the top of the scale, so no further escalation is required.
revised_comments: Rural primary schools in the Central African Republic keep day-to-day pupil records - attendance registers, grade books and enrolment lists - on paper, but school principals also submit periodic enrolment and attendance data directly to the Ministry of Education via the EduTrac SMS-based reporting system, introduced in 2019 under the Global Partnership for Education's Accelerated Funding Programme and still in use as of 2023. This SMS channel provides a real-time digital data feed from schools into a central web-based Education Management Information System, alongside otherwise paper-based record-keeping at the facility, placing rural primary schools at a stage where most records remain on paper but some data capture is digital. Data quality and coverage remain constrained by limited statistical capacity, weak IT infrastructure and heavy dependence on external donor funding.
